What makes the profile unusual is the sprint speed at 29.5 ft/s, 96th percentile, paired with that kind of raw power; most players with that exit velocity profile don't also project for 39 stolen bases. The one real tension is a 34.1% chase rate, 23rd percentile, meaning pitchers will keep testing him out of the zone, and if he can't tighten that, the strikeout number climbs and the .277 projection starts to look optimistic. If the chase rate holds or improves, you've got a genuine 44-homer, 39-steal talent at 24, the kind of profile that ages into an MVP conversation.

reports.name: Junior Caminero
reports.published_report: Forty-four projected home runs at age 23, and the contact quality behind it is not a mirage: 92.8 mph average exit velocity, a 50.0% hard-hit rate, and an xSLG of .496 that suggests the current .532 SLG projection is well within reach once you account for park and sequencing luck. The whole profile lives on the bat, which is fine, because the bat is genuinely loud. Fielding OAA sits at the first percentile and sprint speed at 26.6 ft/s, so if Tampa ever decides third base isn't workable, the power has to carry a DH profile without the defensive value propping up his roster standing. The read here is straightforward: if the 11.4% walk rate holds and the 18.2% strikeout rate stays where it is, this is a middle-of-the-order corner bat who hits 44 home runs and posts a near-.900 OPS deep into his prime.

reports.name: Jackson Merrill
reports.published_report: The xSLG sits at .490 — legitimate raw power, borne out by a 12.8% barrel rate and 48.3% hard-hit rate that both grade well above the league median. The problem is he earns almost none of it for free: a 36.8% chase rate and 6.4% walk rate mean pitchers can expand the zone and make him beat them, which caps the ceiling on a projection line that already has .300 OBP as the number doing the most damage. Speed at 29.0 ft/s translates cleanly into the 28 stolen bases the projection carries, so the counting-stat floor stays comfortable even when the plate discipline drags. If he ever narrows the zone, this profile jumps; if he doesn't, he's a productive, slightly frustrating middle-of-the-order piece who runs his way into value.

reports.name: Sal Stewart
reports.published_report: Thirty-four home runs projected across a full season at 22 years old is the headline, but the Statcast profile explains why it's believable: Stewart barrels the ball at a 12.9% rate and posts an xSLG of .477, both sitting in the 86th percentile, while his xwOBA lands at .350. The contact quality is legitimate even though the hard-hit rate at 39.9% reads as ordinary, because he finds barrels more consistently than he finds pure exit velocity, a skill set that ages well if his chase and whiff rates, currently around league average, don't deteriorate as pitchers probe him further. If the discipline holds, you're looking at a .268/.338/.475 corner bat with middle-of-the-order RBI volume; if he gets exposed in the zone, the floor is a masher who needs to be platooned.

reports.name: Elly De La Cruz
reports.published_report: The exit velocity is 94.6 mph, 99th percentile, and that's where the whole argument starts. De La Cruz barrels the ball at a 16.1% rate, hard-hits it 53.1% of the time, and the expected outcomes line up honestly with what he's actually doing: .373 xwOBA, .499 xSLG, both in the 93rd to 94th percentile range. The one real tension is that 27.4% strikeout rate, which sits in the 13th percentile, meaning the raw contact issues aren't a scouting whisper but a Statcast confirmation. If the swing decisions sharpen even modestly, his 10.8% walk rate suggests he's not lost up there, you get a .281/.360/.508 line with 29 home runs and 28 stolen bases in a full season, which is legitimate MVP-conversation production at shortstop. If the whiff rate climbs instead of falls, the power still plays but the average erodes and the upside shrinks to a good-not-great middle-of-the-order bat.

reports.published_report: The contact quality is almost beyond argument: a .297 xBA sitting at the 99th percentile, a 53.9% hard-hit rate, 92.9 mph average exit velocity. reports.name: Jackson Chourio

At 91.7 mph average exit velocity with a 12.4% barrel rate, Chourio hits the ball as hard as almost anyone his age, and the .476 xSLG reflects that. The projection's 25 home runs in 579 plate appearances feels honest rather than generous, but he's chasing at 34.1%, a rate that lands near the bottom quarter of the league, and until that improves the contact ceiling stays capped below what the raw power suggests. If he tightens the zone, he's a legitimate middle-of-the-order force at 22; if the chase rate holds, he's a high-SLG, high-strikeout outfielder, still useful and dangerous, just not the star the exit velo says he could be.

reports.name: James Wood
reports.published_report: The contact-to-power translation looks exactly right once you see the Statcast shape: 95.2 mph average exit velocity and a 20.3% barrel rate both sitting at the 100th percentile, paired with a 16.9% walk rate that almost no hitter in the sport matches. A 28.5% K% at the 11th percentile is the one lever that determines whether he's a true star or merely a very good one, and the 30.3% whiff rate explains where it comes from. The chase discipline is elite but the bat-to-ball isn't, and if the whiff rate compresses even modestly, the .391 OBP projection and .569 xSLG both make sense without requiring any leap of faith. That's a 32-homer, 110-run profile with 23 stolen bases on top, and the underlying contact quality is already there in the Statcast data — the swing-and-miss is the only thing that caps how high this goes.

reports.name: Jacob Misiorowski

The fastball sits 100.6 mph with 2633 rpm of spin, and hitters are whiffing at 37.4%, which explains why barrels are down to 3.9% and average exit velocity is 87.1 mph: they're not making meaningful contact when they do connect. reports.name: Shohei Ohtani
reports.published_report: The contact profile has a wrinkle worth naming: a 31.5% whiff rate sits near the bottom of the league while the .399 xwOBA and .554 xSLG sit at the very top of it, which means he's generating elite expected damage on contact while giving away more swings than you'd expect from a hitter this good. That tension resolves in his favor because a 15.8% barrel rate and 93.2 mph average exit velocity say the contact, when it lands, is genuinely punishing. On the mound, the 2.73 xERA and 30.4% whiff rate against hitters describe a true ace, and 98.1 mph on the fastball is the foundation that makes the strikeout rate credible. The whole profile hinges on health and workload management across both roles, but when both sides are active, the Statcast read is the same in either direction: a front-of-the-rotation starter and a middle-of-the-order bat occupying the same roster spot.

reports.name: Jordan Walker
reports.published_report: The contact skills and the plate discipline are pulling hard against each other. Walker's 92.5 mph average exit velocity and 49.0% hard-hit rate represent genuine plus contact quality, but a 35.8% chase rate and 31.4% whiff rate are the brakes on all of it. At .280/.336/.485 with 30 home runs and 20 steals across 672 projected plate appearances, he profiles as a productive everyday outfielder, and the underlying Statcast contact grades make that line believable. The whole profile hinges on whether pitchers learn to live up in the zone against him; if the chase rate keeps climbing, the .280 average erodes and the .821 OPS goes with it, and what's left is a middle-of-the-order bat that never quite delivers on the raw.

reports.name: Eli Willits
reports.published_report: The walk rate is the loudest thing in the profile. Eli Willits has drawn 95 walks across AA & A+ & A this season at 18 years old, an 18% clip that translates to 12.7% at the MLB level, and the .406 OBP it produces in the minors is the direct result of that discipline, not a BABIP mirage at .327. The power is the real question at the next level: his .198 ISO across AA & A+ & A translates to .134 in MLB terms, a figure that sits below what the average big-league hitter produces, so the everyday-regular ceiling hinges on whether the raw power develops or he settles in as a high-OBP shortstop whose 62 stolen bags keep him in lineups regardless. If the bat authority doesn't grow, you're looking at a second-division regular who gets on base and runs, which isn't nothing for a shortstop this age.

reports.name: Kade Anderson
reports.published_report: A 1.1 ERA and a 0.6 WHIP at Double-A aren't numbers that need context — they're the argument. Anderson has struck out 135 batters against 13 walks across 93.3 innings at AA this season, and the command profile translates cleanly: a BB/9 of 2.0 in MLB terms, well below the 3.2 figure where most pitchers land, with a K-BB% that comes out to 21.9% against an average of 13.5%. The whole thing hinges on whether the stuff backs up the control at the highest level, because a left-hander this young who misses this many bats while almost never missing the zone has no obvious developmental ceiling short of a frontline starter. If the stuff softens in the jump, he's still a useful mid-rotation arm, but nothing in this line suggests you should expect softening.

reports.name: Gage Wood
reports.published_report: The K-BB% across AA & A is 27%, and that's the number that makes Gage Wood worth watching. He's struck out 139 across 95 innings while walking just 30, and when you level-adjust that profile, the K/9 translates to 9.6 at the MLB level, a full strikeout per nine above where the average MLB arm sits. The concern is the walk rate: his MLB-equivalent BB/9 of 3.3 lands almost exactly at the MLB mean, meaning the command that looks clean in the minors flattens almost entirely once you translate it, and if walks creep even a tick in a big-league zone, the strikeouts have to carry the full load. If the stuff plays up, he's a rotation starter; if the walk rate drifts and the strikeouts don't fully translate, what's left is a depth arm.

reports.name: Cade Cavalli
reports.published_report: The 28.2% strikeout rate is the engine here, sitting at a level most starting pitchers don't reach, and his 96.8 mph fastball explains how he gets there. What the Statcast profile reveals is a gap between the strikeout profile and the contact damage: a 40.3% hard-hit rate that the xERA of 3.72 is already baking in, and which the projection's 3.14 ERA is choosing to look past. That ERA over 177.5 innings hinges almost entirely on 207 strikeouts doing the damage control that contact suppression isn't doing. If the strikeout rate holds, he's a legitimate mid-rotation arm; if it slips, that hard-hit exposure has nowhere to hide.

reports.name: Juneiker Caceres
reports.published_report: The contact-and-patience combo at 18 is doing real work: a 14% strikeout rate against a 13% walk rate across A+ & A, with 46 strikeouts and 43 walks in 337 plate appearances. That discipline translates to a 19.3% K% and 9.5% BB% at the MLB-equivalent level, both better than the MLB mean, which means there's a real floor here even if the power never fully arrives. The .183 ISO across A+ & A is the honest caveat — it translates to .126 at the MLB equivalent, well shy of average, and the ceiling as a bench or platoon bat depends almost entirely on whether that gap closes as he matures. If it doesn't, what remains is a patient, high-contact corner outfielder whose future sits closer to the org depth floor than anything else.

reports.name: Andrew Fischer
reports.published_report: Forty-eight home runs across AA & A+ with a .384 ISO and 102 walks in 556 plate appearances — the raw production is loud enough that the real debate is whether the strikeout rate survives the translation. It doesn't improve: Fischer's 33% clip at the minor-league level moves to 34.7% against MLB pitching, where the average club sits around 22%, and that's the number the whole profile hangs on. The walk rate translates cleanly to 13.8%, well clear of the MLB norm of 8.5%, and the power (.244 ISO equivalent) gives him a floor even if the strikeouts stay ugly. If he trims the whiffs even modestly, he's a regular; if 34.7% is the floor, you're looking at a platoon bat who gets exposed and lives off power peaks.

reports.name: Ezequiel Duran
reports.published_report: The Statcast profile here is a treadmill: contact quality sits around the 33rd percentile in xSLG and the 27th in xwOBA, the chase rate is a bottom-sixth problem at 35.8%, and yet the projection still gets to 18 home runs and .266 across 595 PA because 28.9 ft/s sprint speed (88th percentile) manufactures value that the bat alone can't. That's the whole tension in this profile: a below-average contact quality profile propped up by elite legs and what looks like genuinely elite third-base defense. If the speed ages or the OAA (99th percentile) is overstated, you're left with a second-division regular playing on reputation.

reports.name: Nick Gonzales
reports.published_report: The xBA is the tell: .283 at the 92nd percentile, built on elite contact quality relative to where the ball actually lands, which is why a 16.0% strikeout rate can carry a .303 projection without much help from the power side. His 86.1 mph average exit velocity sits in the bottom tier of the league, and a 3.1% barrel rate confirms the projection's 7 home runs aren't a floor — they're about the ceiling. What he is, practically, is a high-average, low-walk, low-power second baseman whose value lives in the gap between what he hits and how hard he hits it, a gap that holds as long as pitchers can't systematically exploit the 31.1% chase rate before he makes contact.

reports.name: Brooks Lee
reports.published_report: The Statcast profile is almost entirely a warning label. His xwOBA sits at .276 and his xBA at .225, both bottom-fifth marks, driven by a 34.0% hard-hit rate and a 4.3% barrel rate that leave almost no margin for error on contact quality. The one thing working in his favor is a 16.3% strikeout rate, which is genuinely good, but a 5.9% walk rate means the plate discipline doesn't translate into on-base value the way it needs to. The projection's 25 home runs against a .298 OBP tells you exactly what he is: a guy whose power output probably flatters the underlying contact profile, and if the .431 SLG doesn't hold up against a chase rate in the bottom quarter of the league, what's left is a low-end regular whose bat plays below the position.

reports.name: Shane McClanahan
reports.published_report: The Statcast profile tells an uncomfortable story: a 4.28 xERA and 8.9% barrel rate allowed after Tommy John surgery, where the stuff-to-contact translation has clearly slipped. The 26.8% whiff rate and 31.6% chase rate say the weapons are still functional, but a K% of 21.8 is modest for a front-of-rotation arm, and hitters are squaring him up at a rate that doesn't match what the projection asks him to do. ValuCast sees a 3.36 ERA over 121.4 innings, which is optimistic if the underlying contact quality doesn't improve, and it hinges entirely on whether the barrel suppression numbers move back toward where they were before the injury.

reports.name: Coby Mayo

Mayo's average exit velocity sits at 91.3 mph with a 13.1% barrel rate, and his xSLG of .466 grades in the 83rd percentile — the raw power is legitimate, translated into the shape of contact he's making. reports.name: Logan Henderson
reports.published_report: A 2.61 xERA with a 4.6% walk rate is an elite combination, and the Statcast profile doesn't hide the mechanism: Henderson isn't missing bats at a rate that explains the results, with a 26.9% whiff rate and 31.8% chase rate both sitting in the middle of the league. What he does instead is locate, relentlessly, with a fastball that isn't moving hitters off the plate by velocity alone and a contact profile that stays quiet because he simply doesn't give hitters anything dangerous to swing at. The 30.2% strikeout rate and a barrel rate well below average convert into that .251 xwOBA, which the projection largely trusts — 2.55 ERA over 101.6 innings, 11 wins, a 0.83 WHIP. reports.name: Jaiden Lo Re
reports.published_report: The contact-and-walk profile is already elite for a 19-year-old, and that's the uncomfortable truth about this one. Across A+ & A this season, he's running a 10% strikeout rate against a 15% walk rate in 292 plate appearances, and those translate to a 16.8% K rate and 10.6% walk rate at the MLB level, both better than a league where the average hitter punches out 22% of the time. The power is where the ceiling closes: a .120 ISO across A+ & A that translates to .105, well shy of the MLB average of .150, and the 19 stolen bases are the compensating tool that keeps the profile from reading as one-dimensional. If the bat-to-ball gift and speed hold as he climbs, he's either a bench bat or a platoon piece at the top; if the power never comes, the bench is the ceiling, not the floor.

reports.name: Connor Prielipp
reports.published_report: The strikeout rate and the contact quality are pulling in opposite directions, and that tension is the whole profile. Prielipp sits at 24.0% K% in his current MLB sample, which is functional, but his 41.5% Hard-Hit% and 90.2 mph average exit velocity tell you hitters are squaring him up when they do make contact, and the 5.10 ERA the projection carries reflects exactly that gap. The xERA of 4.10 is kinder, but a 23.6% Whiff% suggests the chase-and-miss tool isn't sharp enough to consistently change that contact shape. If the fastball at 95.6 mph starts generating more weak contact than it currently does, there's a back-end starter here; if it doesn't, this is a bulk innings arm with a short leash.

reports.name: Heriberto Hernández
reports.published_report: The gap between his contact grades and his raw power is the whole tension in Hernández's profile. His 13.8% barrel rate sits in the 91st percentile and his .487 xSLG clears the 90th, but a 33.5% whiff rate drags his xBA all the way down to .246, which is why he projects to a .225 average over 494 plate appearances despite an average exit velocity of 91.5 mph. The swing-and-miss is the load-bearing problem: if the 27.1% strikeout rate doesn't come down, the 26 projected home runs and .310 OBP will be a ceiling rather than a floor, and he looks more like a streaky bench bat than the everyday corner outfielder the underlying power grades suggest he could be. His 24.2% chase rate is encouragingly restrained, meaning the whiff damage is happening on pitches he swings at rather than ones he's fishing for, which gives the contact problem a mechanical shape rather than a recognition one.

reports.name: Daniel Espino

Twenty-two free passes in that same stretch translate to a 4.3 BB/9, more than a full walk per nine above what the average MLB arm allows, which is why the K-BB% lands at just 13.6% in MLB terms, barely a tick above the league mean. Everything here hinges on whether he can convert strikeout stuff into actual strike-throwing, because right now the command profile strips the margin from the ERA and leaves a depth arm floor with a depth arm ceiling. reports.name: Bryce Harper
reports.published_report: The .388 xwOBA tells you most of what you need to know: Harper is producing at an elite level regardless of what ball-in-play luck has done to his batting average. The mechanism is almost entirely discipline, a 16.1% walk rate at the 98th percentile paired with a chase rate low enough that pitchers rarely get him to expand. His whiff rate of 30.5% is genuinely elevated and the power contact metrics are mid-tier rather than monstrous, so what he's doing is manufacturing premium offensive value through selectivity and damage on the pitches he chooses to swing at, not by overpowering the baseball. The projection of .271/.385/.497 over 691 plate appearances is what a healthy, full-season version of this profile looks like, and it all hinges on staying on the field and continuing to own the zone the way he currently does.

reports.name: Braylon Doughty
reports.published_report: The walk rate is the whole argument here. Across AA & A+, Doughty has issued just 25 walks in 104.4 innings, a 2.2 BB/9 that translates to 2.7 in MLB terms, comfortably under the MLB average of 3.2. That kind of command at 20 is the thing you can't teach, and the 1.3 WHIP says it's showing up in results. The strikeout side is more modest, 114 punchouts across AA & A+ translating to a 7.9 K/9 where the average MLB starter sits at 8.6, so this isn't a swing-and-miss profile riding a hot stretch, which is exactly why the ceiling lands at multi-inning reliever or setup role rather than something grander. If the command holds as he climbs, he's a useful late-inning weapon; if the stuff doesn't gain enough to bump that K rate, the floor is a depth arm who misses bats just often enough to stay on a roster.

reports.name: Nathan Church
reports.published_report:
The Statcast profile here is mostly a warning label. An 85.8 mph average exit velocity and 29.9% hard-hit rate both sit near the bottom of the league, and an xwOBA of .289 is about as thin as a starting outfielder's contact profile can get before the roster math stops working.

What keeps him alive is the 42.3% chase rate — that number is the whole problem in a single figure, because a guy chasing that often with soft contact is giving pitchers every reason to stay outside the zone forever. The 17.4% strikeout rate looks fine in isolation, but that's because he's making weak contact on pitches he shouldn't swing at rather than taking them, and the 5.6% walk rate confirms he isn't winning the exchange.

Speed at 28.5 ft/s and a solid fielding mark give him a place on a roster, but the projection's .297 OBP across 457 PA tells you exactly the ceiling here: a useful fourth outfielder who can run and cover ground, and not much more.

reports.name: Bubba Chandler
reports.published_report:
98.4 mph fastball, 11.6% walk rate. That's Bubba Chandler's profile in two numbers, and they pull in opposite directions hard enough to explain everything else.

The contact suppression is genuinely encouraging: a 5.7% barrel rate is well above average, and hitters are doing real damage on very few balls. But the strikeout and whiff numbers are modest for someone throwing that hard, which points to the walks as the root problem — when you're not missing bats at a high clip, a 11.6% walk rate means you're constantly working from behind and the good contact you're avoiding starts mattering less.

The xERA of 4.02 and a projection of 4.26 ERA over 154.8 innings land him squarely as a back-end starter right now, the kind of arm whose ceiling depends entirely on whether the command tightens enough to let the fastball be a weapon rather than a liability.

reports.name: Kyle Stowers

Stowers hits the ball as hard as almost anyone, a 92.4 mph average exit velocity and 56.3% hard-hit rate that together put him in rarefied company for raw impact, yet a 36.2% whiff rate and 32.3% strikeout rate mean a huge fraction of plate appearances never reach that exit velocity at all. The .329 xwOBA and .436 xSLG say the damage accumulates when contact happens; the .229 xBA says it doesn't happen often enough to hide the swing-and-miss. Project him into a full season and the 21-homer, .789 OPS outcome is there, but if the strikeout rate keeps the barrel rate from adding up, what remains is a bench bat with a loud exit velocity chart and not much else.

reports.name: Kevin Alvarez
reports.published_report: The contact and the legs are already there at 18. Across 443 plate appearances at A ball, Alvarez is hitting .261/.343/.429 with 17 stolen bases, and his 18% strikeout rate ranks in the 82nd percentile among the hitter pool, a genuine skill at his age on a real sample. The translation is the problem: that .168 ISO at A ball shrinks to .116 in MLB-equivalent context, a number that sits noticeably short of where average power lands, and an 8% walk rate doesn't add enough margin to paper over thin game power. If the power develops, and at 18 in full-season ball there's room to dream, he's a second-division regular with speed and a real hit tool; if it doesn't, he's a bench piece who runs well and makes contact, which isn't nothing, but it's the ceiling not the floor.

Across 127 innings and 26 starts at AA, the sample is substantial; the problem is what it shows: a lefty whose stuff misses bats but not enough of the zone to survive a step up. Everything here points to a depth arm, and it stays a depth arm unless the command tightens in a way the full-season AA line hasn't suggested it will.

Bagwell has issued 32 walks against 105 strikeouts in 108 innings, and that command profile lands in the 91st percentile against his peer group — the contact management is real enough that his 95th-percentile WHIP isn't a mirage. The problem is the strikeout rate: 8.7 K/9 at these levels translates to a 6.8 at the MLB equivalent, well short of the 8.6 that passes for average up there, and a pitcher who controls the zone but doesn't miss enough bats needs everything else to hold precisely. If the command stays and the stuff ticks up, he's a back-end starter or durable reliever; if the velocity or shape doesn't add swing-and-miss, he's an organizational arm competing for depth work.
